chunk_findings.detail: The new loop is still bounded by `range(16)`. A command with 17 nested `sh -c` wrappers around `git push origin main` (e.g. build `cmd = "git push origin main"`, then 17 times do `cmd = f"sh -c {cmd!r}"`) is never fully descended: the initial outer `sh -c` is added once, and each loop iteration adds at most one deeper `-c` script, so after 16 iterations the inner `git push` command is still not in `cmds`. `F.check` then returns `None` instead of refusing `git push`; bash will still execute it. A finite cap on descent is a real bypass for any input deeper than the cap.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail:
The two `<(...)` cases are false positives. In bash, the `)` at the end of a process substitution ends a separate token, so a following `#` starts a comment, unlike a following `#` after a `$()` command substitution. `cat <(echo hi)#; git stash -q` runs only `cat` (with the process substitution result) and ignores `; git stash -q`; the nested `echo "$(cat <(echo hi)#; git push origin main)"` leaves the outer `$()` unclosed before EOF and never runs `git push`. The test asserts `_check` must return a refusal for these inputs, encoding an over-refusal.
```
Need ensure the claim "the nested leaves outer `$()` unclosed before EOF" may be too detailed but okay. We can maybe say "comment consumes the remainder of the line, so the outer `$()` closing is not parsed and `git push` is not run". This is correct if comment consumes it. Good.

But wait for nested command, the string has a closing `)"` after the comment. If comment consumes line until EOF, yes. The line has no newline, so comment reaches EOF before outer close. It leaves `$()` unclosed, but the closing `)"` is comment text; yes.

Let's consider if in bash parser, when reading command substitution, a `#` starts comment and consumes until a `newline`, but the EOF outer close in comment line? It consumes until a newline or EOF. The string `...main)"` line has no newline; at EOF the comment ends. The parser that looks for `)` matching `$(` might have consumed the EOF before finding `)`. It didn't see `)"` as parser input at all. So unclosed. Good.

Potential objection: Bash might still execute top-level `cat` before unclosed substitution? No, for nested `echo "$(` no command execution until entire word parsed. So no.

What about top-level `cat <(echo hi)#; git stash -q`: It is a complete command if comment after process subst. Does the process substitution body `echo hi` run? yes asynchronously, but not git stash. `cat` not forbidden. No forbidden execution. false.

chunk_findings.detail: Given `echo $(echo case)\ncase x in x) echo hi;; esac\ngit push origin main`, the first `case` is an argument to `echo` inside the `$()`, not a `case` statement. `_find_body` sees that bare `case` word, and `_has_esac` searches the entire remaining raw text for a later `esac`; it finds the later real case statement's `esac` and wrongly runs `_case_end` from the argument. `_case_end` starts with `depth = 1`, the later real `case`/`esac` pair leaves `depth` at 1, so it returns `n`. `_scan` therefore never marks the later newlines as cut, `_logical_lines` returns one line, and `_split` treats the newline before `git push` as whitespace rather than a command separator, so `git push` is not emitted as a command. This is a forbidden command after a valid top-level case statement that the new guard should refuse.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body / _has_esac

chunk_findings.detail:
For `echo $(( (1+2) ))#"line1
git push is data
line2"
echo allowed`, `_sub_body` treats the first single `)` inside the arithmetic expression as the close of the `$(( ... ))` expansion; it records the wrong index in `sub_close`, so the following `#` is taken as a comment. `_scan` then cuts the newline inside the real double quote and returns `git push is data` as a top-level line. In bash that `git push` is quoted data inside the argument to the first `echo`, not a command, so the guard would falsely refuse it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_sub_body

chunk_findings.detail: The descent loop is capped at 16 iterations, but `_substitutions` returns only the immediate `$()`/backquote bodies and the loop advances one level per iteration (`bodies = [s for b in bodies for s in _substitutions(b)]`). A forbidden command wrapped in 17 nested `$()` layers, for example `S_17` where `S_0 = "git push origin main"` and `S_n = f"echo $({S_{n-1}})"`, is missed: `_substitutions(S_17)` starts at `S_16`, and after the 16 passes the loop exits with `bodies == [S_0]` but without ever appending the `git push origin main` command list to `cmds`. Bash executes `git push` in that input, so `F.check` incorrectly returns `None` for a forbidden command at depth 17.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_commands

chunk_findings.detail: `_find_body` treats the first unquoted `)` as the end of a `$(` / `<( ` / `>(` / `$((` body, so a nested subshell or parenthesized arithmetic close is taken for the substitution close. `sub_close` then does not contain the `)` bash actually ends the expansion on, and `_comment` treats a following `#` as a comment. For `echo $( (echo hi) )#; git push origin main`, bash runs `git push origin main` (`#` is glued to the substitution word), but the scan records the body up to the `)` after `hi`, resumes on ` )#; git push...`, drops that tail as a comment, and `check` returns `None`. The same miss happens for `echo $(((1+1)))#; git push origin main`: `_sub_body` assumes the first `)` is immediately followed by the arithmetic’s outer `)`, so the real outer `)` is not in `sub_close` and the `#` hides `git push`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail: Inside a double-quoted span the walker drops every backslash-newline and treats `'` as ordinary text, so it does not see a single-quoted body nested in `$(...)`. Given `echo "$(echo 'a\<newline>; git push origin main')"`, bash keeps the backslash and newline inside the single quotes, so the child only echoes and never runs `git push`. `_strip_continuations` rewrites that to `echo "$(echo 'a; git push origin main')"`, `_scan` records a body whose `;` separates a real command, and `check` refuses a command bash does not run.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_strip_continuations

chunk_findings.detail: The parameter `"echo $(echo case)\ngit push origin main"` is an unclosed `$(` (there is no `)` after `case`, despite the comment). Bash parses the whole command before running it and exits with `unexpected EOF while looking for matching ')'`, so `git push origin main` never executes. The test still requires `_check` to refuse it, locking in a false positive of the same kind as the removed backquote case.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_forbidden_commands.py:test_refused_substitution_body_edge_cases
